The app already has the underlying pieces—Rust-owned persistence, Gmail sync, durable archive/read actions, and local drafts—but its UI is still a basic inbox/reader/activity layout.

I’d build the new browsing experience on those foundations, starting with focus → open → read → back, then adding triage, discovery, and broader mailbox workflows. The plan will also flag deliberate departures from the spec: opening currently never marks mail read, and reminders, attachment previews, and multiple accounts extend beyond the accepted first-build scope.

| Decision | This document's position |
|---|---|
| macOS-first target | Approved for the Slice 02 disposable-account pilot; platform smoke remains pending |
| Gmail REST provider | Implemented read-only in Slice 02; do not infer broader provider capabilities |
| Fork vs greenfield | Greenfield pattern-reuse recommended; final commit at scaffolding |
| Exact dependencies/versions | Chosen at scaffolding; none claimed here |
| `tauri-specta` adoption | Evaluate at scaffolding against the chosen Tauri version |
| SQLite library and FTS approach | Chosen at scaffolding; verify capabilities rather than assume |
| OAuth app registration (personal vs verified status) | Resolve before stage 2; see README OAuth notes |
| Hide vs quit default UX | Decide and document in UI during stage 1–2 |

## 12. References

- [ADR 0001](docs/adr/0001-single-account-desktop-email-client.md) — governing first-build scope and safety gates.
- [PRD](PRD.md) — long-term direction; §7 security boundaries, §10 architecture direction.
- [email security review](security/email-review.md), [Pebble security review](security/pebble-review.md) — defect patterns this design must outpace (durable staging, unknown outcomes, renderer isolation).
- [README](README.md) — historical research: candidate comparison, Tauri tradeoffs, OAuth notes.
- Official [Tauri 2 capabilities](https://v2.tauri.app/security/capabilities/) — the app-command restriction nuance in §8.
- Official [Vue](https://vuejs.org/guide/introduction.html),
  [TanStack Query](https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/vue/overview), and
  [Vitest](https://vitest.dev/) documentation — frontend stack references.

# Superhuman-inspired browsing: incremental implementation plan

**Status:** Proposed roadmap, not an implementation contract or authorization to access real mail.

Source: [Superhuman Email Browsing UX Specification](../superhuman-email-browsing-ux-spec.md).
Existing constraints: [ADR 0001](adr/0001-single-account-desktop-email-client.md),
[development guide](development.md), and implementation contracts for
[Slices 01](vertical-slice-01.md), [02](vertical-slice-02.md),
[03](vertical-slice-03.md), and [04](vertical-slice-04.md).

## Recommendation

Build the browsing experience around the existing mail foundation, not as a replacement backend or a screenshot-only frontend. Deliver a working user journey in each slice:

```text
User input → Vue interaction state → typed MailClient/Tauri boundary
           → Rust query/command → SQLite/provider where needed
           → authoritative result/change hint → visible state and recovery
```

Start with **focus → open → read → back** in the new layout. Then introduce discovery, reversible triage, bulk processing, a saved split, and historical search. Stop at that useful browsing milestone before expanding into the broader mailbox-management features.

Use `UX-01` onward below to avoid confusing this roadmap with the repository's existing numbered implementation slices. These are delivery increments, not separate architectural layers. A slice must not wait for a later "backend integration" or "testing phase" to become useful.

## 1. What exists and what must change

Source inspection, not a new runtime certification:

| Area | Current implementation | Consequence for this plan |
|---|---|---|
| Foundation | Vue 3/TypeScript, thin Tauri 2 shell, Rust `mail-core`, SQLite | Preserve the stack and narrow typed boundaries |
| Mail access | Explicit single-account Gmail profile; bounded discovery of up to 100 conversations; plain-text cache; sync and freshness reporting | Cached rows are not the entire mailbox; browsing/search/counts need explicit coverage |
| Actions | Durable archive/unarchive and explicit read/unread; immutable message targets, idempotency, reconciliation, Activity | Reuse execution machinery; Undo, groups, stars, labels, trash, etc. are new work |
| Drafts | Local-only composer, revisioned saves, safe reply preparation, native close/quit protocol | Rehouse rather than rewrite; preserve dirty-buffer and close protections |
| Layout | `App.vue` mounts list, reader, Activity, account and drafts panels; `style.css` has a multi-column utility layout | New list/reader modes and contact pane are a real layout change, not merely new colors |
| Focus | `useMailbox.ts` exposes `selectedIndex`, preserving identity during refresh; `InboxList.vue` treats focus as selection | Introduce explicit ID-based conversation focus, separate from future bulk selection |
| Reader | All plain-text messages expanded; no separate message focus | Add message focus/expansion without changing safe rendering or reply-source rules |
| Discovery | Inbox-only `listConversations()`; no search, split definitions, folder/label catalog, palette, or contact pane | Add bounded queries as the relevant slice needs them |
| Tests | Rust synthetic provider/storage tests; Vitest component/transport tests; in-memory browser fake | No existing real-browser E2E runner; fake IPC tests do not validate the native bridge |

Primary change points:

- `src/App.vue`, `src/assets/style.css`, `src/components/InboxList.vue`, `ReaderView.vue`, `ActivityPanel.vue`.
- `src/composables/useMailbox.ts`; retain `useDrafts.ts`'s persistence/lifecycle responsibilities.
- `src/lib/ipc/client.ts`, `tauri-client.ts`, `browser-fake.ts`.
- `crates/mail-core/src/dto.rs`, `store.rs`, `gmail/{types,provider,store,sync,operations}.rs`.
- `src-tauri/src/main.rs`, command manifest/permissions and capabilities whenever IPC changes.
- `src/lib/ipc/generated.ts` remains generated from Rust, never hand-maintained.

Do not reorganize the whole repository, add a state framework, build a generic workflow engine, or replace the worker before delivering the first journey.

## 2. Scope and fidelity decisions

1. **Evidence remains visible.** Implement visual/documented (`V`/`D`) requirements; treat proposed (`P`) interactions as our chosen contracts. Keep unresolved (`U`) fidelity questions in a checklist. Passing our tests does not establish behavioral equivalence to Superhuman.
2. **Keep opening non-mutating.** The app's explicit no-auto-read policy stays. The spec permits, but does not require, marking a loaded conversation read. Any later automatic-read policy needs a separate decision, capability checks, and tests.
3. **Single-account Gmail first.** Keep account identity on every reference, but do not build Outlook or multi-account infrastructure to demonstrate abstraction. Hide unsupported commands rather than implementing inert controls.
4. **Preserve the composer.** Composition/sending behavior is outside this browsing plan. New draft/Reply remain exits into the existing local-only editor; do not add sending or weaken source-message validation.
5. **Stay plain-text initially.** No `v-html`, remote avatars, tracking pixels, fabricated contact enrichment, or HTML rendering in the privileged app DOM. Attachment previews and HTML fidelity have separate security gates.
6. **Treat the larger spec as a roadmap, not a silent ADR replacement.** Saved splits/search fit the accepted first build. Broader labels/actions need explicit implementation contracts; reminders, attachment previews, and native multi-account tabs require updates to ADR 0001's explicit deferrals before implementation. AI, calendar and mobile remain excluded.
7. **No new mailbox authority is implied.** Planning a label/trash/unsubscribe action does not authorize operating it on a real account. Preserve the existing permission upgrade and disposable-account gates.

## 3. Minimal shared design, introduced incrementally

### Separate mail state from browsing state

Rust/SQLite continues to own cached provider facts, durable intent, view definitions and operation history. Vue owns navigation, focus, selected IDs, expansion, scroll anchors and overlays. Backend events remain invalidation hints, not the source of truth.

Introduce the state needed by each slice, rather than landing the entire spec's state model first:

- UX-01: focused conversation **reference**, open reference, list scroll anchor and reader origin.
- UX-02: active message ID and expanded message IDs, scoped to a conversation visit.
- UX-03: context/history and a topmost overlay; initially only inbox and cached Done.
- UX-05: selected references and range anchor, independent of focus.
- UX-06/07: saved-split/search contexts, query/filter and result-page identity.
- UX-13 only: independent per-workspace browsing state and multiple accounts.

Always key by account plus conversation/message identity, not array position. Compute an index only for adjacent movement. Clear invalid focus/contact/action targets on empty results and invalidate stale requests on account/context changes.

### One action catalog, not a generic executor

Introduce a small frontend command registry in UX-03. Buttons, shortcuts and palette entries share action IDs, labels, shortcuts, availability and target resolution. The execution path still invokes named typed IPC commands; never expose `execute`, arbitrary SQL, HTTP, filesystem or arbitrary provider-label mutation.

Dispatch precedence: system/browser reservations → top overlay → editor/IME/native controls → reader message commands → conversation actions → inbox-only split navigation. Intercept `Tab` only when the inbox conversation surface owns it, never globally. Escape dismisses the top surface, then selection, then reader/search context. Do not steal focus during background refreshes.

### Extend query contracts when contexts arrive

In UX-03 introduce a bounded browsing request/result alongside, or compatibly extending, the current inbox query. It should carry:

- A validated context, later filter/query, and opaque pagination cursor.
- Account-scoped conversation summaries with stable ordering and IDs.
- Coverage/freshness: cached versus provider results, whether more pages exist, and whether an exact total is known.
- Separate loaded-row count from any exact total count. Unknown is not zero.

The backend verifies the active account; caller-supplied IDs do not authorize another account. Provider searches/folder reads use their own bounded result/cache policy and must not reset inbox discovery/history checkpoints or evict operation recovery snapshots. Freeze details in the relevant slice contract, not all future APIs now.

## 4. Delivery sequence

### UX-01 — A compact inbox that can actually be browsed

**Journey:** Launch → move focus with J/K → see the correspondent → Enter/click → read → Escape/back to the same row and scroll position.

- Build the rail, compact top navigation and warm-dark tokens from the spec. Use constrained sender width, a one-line subject/snippet, trailing date/actions, lavender focus bar, nonselectable date groups and generous unused space below short lists.
- List mode shows contact context, not a message preview. Reader mode replaces the central list surface; rail and contact context remain. Account/Activity/drafts become explicit accessible surfaces instead of permanent competing columns. Keep freshness, pending/error indicators and recovery discoverable.
- Convert `selectedIndex` into explicit focused identity. Hover must not change focus/read state; inline actions stop propagation. Preserve existing archive/recovery controls and permission gates during the layout change.
- Render only known contact fields. Add a minimal backend-derived primary correspondent to the summary if needed; do not fetch an entire body on every J/K movement or guess the latest sender from the unordered participant list. No external enrichment.
- Use real cached/core data through existing list/detail IPC. Additive DTO changes require generator and transport tests. No new provider writes.

**E2E checkpoint:** Use a six-conversation synthetic scenario with long names, mixed read states and missing profile fields. Focus the fourth row, open it, return, and verify row identity, list scroll and contact context. Insert a newer row while focused: an action must still target the original ID. Test empty/loading/error states and narrow-desktop contact disclosure.

**Acceptance:** BROWSE-01, 05 (conversation portion), 17, 20. Screenshot measurements are image coordinates, not established CSS pixels; calibrate on the Mac rather than asserting pixel parity.

### UX-02 — Read a multi-message conversation without losing your place

**Journey:** Open a conversation → N/P between messages → O/Shift+O expand → inspect participant details → J/K to another conversation → return to the originating list.

- Add message focus, expansion and a purple focus cue; newest relevant message initially expanded. Use the existing cached message stack and safe text rendering.
- Keep reader scrolling separate from rail/header. Preserve expansion and scroll during background refresh and within the current visit; prune IDs removed remotely.
- Provide full known From/To/timestamps via disclosure. Hover/focus participant context temporarily, restore on exit; contact copy controls must not trigger navigation or drafting.
- J/K in the reader follows its originating list/context, not all cached mail. Loading a different thread disables stale destructive targets.
- Reply still targets the explicitly displayed latest source under Slice 04's checks; focusing an older message must not silently change the reply contract. Unknown Cc/Bcc/header data is absent, not fabricated.

**E2E checkpoint:** A three-message conversation with a long body, hostile literal markup and multiple participants. Exercise message versus conversation navigation, expansion, participant context, copy, reply exit and Back. Reorder/update the source list while reading; stable IDs and a surviving anchor must win.

**Acceptance:** Complete BROWSE-05; copy portion of 15. HTML-only/incomplete/retained snapshots keep their current disclosures and restrictions.

### UX-03 — Discover actions and navigate to recoverable mail

**Journey:** Cmd+K → “go to Done” → open a cached archived conversation → Back to the exact prior inbox context.

- Introduce the shared action catalog and context-aware keyboard dispatcher. Start with implemented actions only: open/back, Done/Not Done, explicit read controls, account/Activity/drafts destinations, and Inbox/cached Done.
- Palette has an input, keyboard-highlighted results, Enter execution, Escape/focus restoration and shortcut labels/tooltips. Editable controls and IME cannot invoke mailbox shortcuts.
- Left opens a small destination navigator; support `G`, then `E` with a documented proposed timeout. Inbox and cached Done reuse rows/reader and a context history stack.
- Add a Rust read query for known locally archived/recovery conversations, including retained snapshots. Label this coverage honestly: it is not provider-complete Done/All Mail. Do not define Done as every thread lacking INBOX; future Sent/Spam/Trash membership must stay distinct.
- Keep activity history independently retrievable as contexts expand; a filtered list must not accidentally filter out operation failures.

**E2E checkpoint:** Archive a fixture thread, navigate to cached Done through palette and pointer, open it and return. Deny capabilities, delay destination responses and type `e/s/h` in the palette: no wrong-thread mutation. Preserve local drafts and normal-close protection after moving their entry points.

**Acceptance:** BROWSE-10, 20 and folder return/keyboard precedence contracts. Cmd+K must be exercised in WKWebView, not just synthetic key events.

### UX-04 — Process one conversation with trustworthy Undo

**Journey:** E marks Done → row/count/focus update → Z within 10 seconds restores the exact prior target state; explicit read/unread has the same recovery discipline.

- Reuse existing durable setters and authoritative pending overlays. Add a concise notification with Undo and visible pending/confirmed/failed/unknown distinctions; accepted locally is not confirmed remotely.
- Add narrow Rust Undo eligibility/query and command contracts. Persist the original target IDs, prior **per-message** values for the affected dimension, expiry and linkage to the original operation. A UI timer or `setArchived(false)` against the thread's latest inventory is not sufficient.
- Undo atomically cancels still-unclaimed intent where safe, or stages an ordered compensating operation against the immutable targets. It must not touch a new incoming message or independent labels/star/read state.
- Initially support the latest eligible action only. Mixed read facts require restoring each prior value; unknown prior facts are not exactly undoable. Expiry and same-target newer actions are checked in Rust. Uncertain dispatched outcomes remain explicitly uncertain/reconciled, not falsely reported as undone.
- Use `Z`, not native text-editing Cmd+Z. Preserve Activity-based recovery after expiry and on restart.

**E2E checkpoint:** Archive → undo at 9 seconds; reject at expiry; archive last/only row; failure rollback; offline accept → restart → restore/reconcile; a new reply between action and Undo remains untouched. Check mixed read values and an older Undo after a newer same-target action.

**Acceptance:** BROWSE-07, 08. Fake clock/provider tests prove durable semantics; approved disposable-Mac tests prove remote convergence.

### UX-05 — Select and process several conversations safely

**Journey:** X / Shift+J/K / Cmd- or Shift-click select three rows → archive → inspect per-item results → recover failures or Undo the eligible group.

- Add selected-ID set/range anchor and explicit count; focus is not selection. Plain J/K never expands selection. Escape clears selection before leaving the list; changing context clears cross-context selection.
- Actions resolve exactly the selected set, otherwise the current conversation. Inline row actions remain explicitly row-scoped. Bulk read controls use a visible desired state rather than ambiguous mixed-state toggling.
- Add durable bounded group acceptance with member receipts/status, idempotent group request and immutable per-thread message targets. Do not treat frontend `Promise.all` as durable or atomic bulk execution.
- Reuse serial execution/reconciliation. Report accepted, succeeded, failed and unknown members separately; failed IDs remain actionable. Group Undo reuses UX-04's preimages and excludes unsafe/superseded members explicitly.
- “Select all loaded” means loaded rows only. Do not promise cross-page/all-matching selection.

**E2E checkpoint:** Select noncontiguous IDs, insert/reorder mail, archive, fail one member and lose another response. Verify precise targets, separate statuses and recovery after restart; returning from a reader must not widen selection.

**Acceptance:** BROWSE-06 (archive), 18; later star actions reuse the same selection mechanism.

### UX-06 — One real saved split, not a classification engine

**Journey:** Define a sender/domain view → switch Inbox/saved split by pointer or Tab → open/read/archive → see both memberships/counts update → disable the view without deleting mail.

- Implement the ADR's one local saved definition, initially bounded sender/domain criteria, stable ordering and optional hide-when-empty. Persist it in Rust/SQLite; add a small editor, no natural-language authoring.
- Reuse browsing contexts, reader, bulk actions, commands and Undo. Views derive membership and never mutate mail. Overlap with Inbox is intentional, not a duplicate-storage error.
- Define counts as total matching conversations, not unread. Render badges only for exact known totals 1…999; cached-only views disclose that scope, and unavailable mailbox totals are not presented as exact.
- Add single-active unread filter first, with unknown read facts not treated as unread. Choose/document nonwrapping split navigation until live evidence says otherwise. Hidden views remain reachable through the palette.
- Do not invent Important/Other classification from Gmail IMPORTANT or make those mutually exclusive storage folders. Existing-label criteria become available after UX-09.

**E2E checkpoint:** Save → restart → switch → open → archive → undo; verify overlapping views, focus/selection isolation, hiding and disabling. Synthetic exact counts 0/1/999/1000 exercise badge rules; timezone-boundary fixtures exercise date groups.

**Acceptance:** BROWSE-02, 03, 04 plus split membership/configuration contracts. Ship Inbox + one named saved split before broader split configuration.

### UX-07 — Find older mail and return without losing the query

**Journey:** / → enter query → Enter → result → reader → Back to query/results/focus → Back to previous split.

- Add search input/operator guidance and reuse the normal list/reader/action surfaces. Contact-name click becomes sender search; add up to four real recent-email links from a bounded query, not invented history.
- Add account-scoped Rust search and a bounded provider read path for older mail. Online search reaches beyond the 100-conversation inbox window; offline search uses cached content with an incompleteness disclosure. A failed search is not an empty result.
- Define a supported parser/AST for AND, OR, quoted phrases, exclusions and initial From/To/Subject criteria. Reject unsupported syntax visibly; do not silently give cached and provider modes different meanings. Add Cc/Bcc/label operators only when the requisite facts are available. Document fields, date/time and Spam/Trash defaults.
- Page/cancel provider work, guard account/context/query generations, deduplicate by conversation ID, and retain the query while loading details. Respect existing rate pacing and auth/cancellation.
- Bound search cache retention separately from inbox discovery; persist/pin any operation targets/recovery context before evicting results. Opening an uncached result is a visible load, never a substitute thread.

**E2E checkpoint:** Find an archived conversation absent from inbox discovery, page results, inspect it, return and edit the query. Force stale responses, offline incomplete coverage, expired auth, rate limits and a missing result body. Contact copy stays independent of search/draft exits.

**Acceptance:** BROWSE-09, 10, 15, 19 and archive-searchability from 07. This completes the initial browsing milestone; it does not complete the ADR's sending/dogfooding scope.

### UX-08 — Star a conversation and find it in Starred

**Journey:** S (or bulk Star) → indicator → go to Starred → unstar → correct neighbor/Back/Undo.

- Add observed per-message star facts, conversation aggregation, a narrow durable setter and reconciliation. Keep star independent of inbox/read state and feed the same group/Undo/catalog machinery.
- Starred becomes a real browsing destination. Add the starred filter once the facts exist, not before. Unknown/partial star facts must remain distinguishable where they affect correctness.

**E2E checkpoint:** Star archived mail, find it in Starred, unstar while browsing that view, fail/restart/reconcile and verify independent read/inbox facts and bulk scope.

**Acceptance:** Remaining star portion of BROWSE-06 and Starred/filter contracts. New provider writes remain capability- and operator-gated.

### UX-09 — Browse labels/folders, then Label versus Move

**Journey:** Left → label → open → L applies a tag without archiving → V moves by applying the destination and Done → recover.

- First add provider label metadata and paginated read destinations: Sent, provider Drafts, All Mail, Spam, Trash and user labels, alongside Inbox/Done/Starred. Distinguish provider Drafts from app-local drafts. Never imply the 100-row cache covers these folders.
- Introduce label facts/membership and existing-label saved-view/search criteria. Render compact badge metadata. Large catalogs get “Show more”; all destinations remain searchable through the palette.
- Then add narrow validated label-apply/remove and Gmail Move commands. Move's label-plus-archive intent is durable and recoverable as one logical operation, not two unrelated UI calls. Preserve other labels/read/star states and freeze message-level membership semantics.
- Gmail only: do not expose Outlook folder/category semantics as supported. Do not add label create/delete or arbitrary rules just to support browsing.

**E2E checkpoints (separate increments):** First browse an uncached provider label and return. Then apply a label and verify INBOX stays; Move and verify destination plus Done; interrupt between stages, restart and recover without falsely reporting full success.

**Acceptance:** BROWSE-11 and remaining ordinary destination/label contracts. Pending/returned Reminders and Muted arrive only with their actual capabilities.

### UX-10 — Broader triage, one explicit scope at a time

This is a sequence of small optional contracts, **not one large mutation PR**:

1. **Trash/recover:** move to Trash → browse Trash → restore; no permanent-delete or empty-Trash command. Distinguish from Done everywhere, including search membership and Undo.
2. **Mute/unmute and Spam/recover:** separate Gmail-supported actions/destinations, immutable targets and visible recovery. Do not assume removing INBOX reproduces future-message mute behavior; validate provider semantics first.
3. **Manual Important/Other placement:** begin with one-conversation placement and separate view membership. Only then add an explicit sender/domain rule editor and durable local rule evaluation. No automatic classification/AI; no implicit escalation from thread to sender/domain. Disclose local-only rule execution and offline/quit limits.
4. **Unsubscribe/Block:** separate exact external/send/provider effects and sender/domain scope from optional archive/trash. Do not implement these as arbitrary URL opening or silently create a send path. Add only after their specific safety/authority contract; otherwise omit the controls.

Each increment reuses contexts, action scopes, durable intent, groups and recovery. A provider feature being unavailable is a visible capability boundary, not a silent no-op.

**E2E checkpoint per increment:** Exact-target action → destination/provider effect → recover; reject unsupported provider/capability; verify sender/domain scope needs explicit confirmation and does not alter unrelated mail.

**Acceptance:** BROWSE-12 plus Trash/Mute/Spam/Block/Unsubscribe contracts. Blocking semantics are not specified sufficiently to assume parity; establish a product/provider contract before implementation.

### UX-11 — Manual reminders with correct pending and returned states

**Scope gate:** Explicitly revise ADR 0001's reminder deferral before implementation.

**Journey:** H → choose manual time/“if no reply” → pending Reminders folder → simulated clock/reply event → returned Reminders split → cancel/recover.

- Store reminder time/timezone, condition, source message/reply baseline and state durably. Default “if no reply,” offer “regardless,” and treat “someday” as unscheduled.
- Pending reminders and returned reminders are distinct memberships. Scheduling/removing from inbox and returning/recovering are coordinated durable intents, not a frontend timer.
- Freeze what counts as a qualifying reply, DST/time parsing, rescheduling/cancellation races and new-message behavior. Reconcile replies before claiming a no-reply reminder fired; incomplete/offline facts cannot prove no reply.
- Execute while the process runs; on launch, reconcile overdue work idempotently. Make desktop-local/non-cross-device behavior explicit. No promise of execution while fully quit and no calendar UI.

**E2E checkpoint:** Schedule → restart → advance fake clock → fire once; qualifying reply suppresses return, “regardless” does not, “someday” never auto-fires. Test cancellation/failure and simultaneous incoming mail.

**Acceptance:** BROWSE-13 and reminder condition/recovery contracts.

### UX-12 — Safely inspect an attachment and return to the message

**Scope gate:** Attachment preview exceeds ADR 0001's initial download-only scope.

**Journey:** Open attachment chip/Cmd+O chooser → preview PDF → Escape restores exact message/expansion/scroll → unsupported file uses explicit download/external path.

- Add bounded attachment descriptors and Rust-owned authenticated fetch/storage. Keep sender filenames/path traversal, MIME mismatch, size limits, safe save destinations and cancellation explicit.
- Validate a restricted PDF viewing surface with no privileged app IPC, no automatic remote-resource loading and a tested platform sandbox. Do not place a third-party document viewer/raw HTML into the trusted app DOM. Choose the viewer only after a macOS security/compatibility spike; download-only is an honest interim capability.
- Cmd+O offers known links/files without auto-opening one arbitrarily. Add copy/open context menus, validated external protocols and safe external handling; no automatic execution. A displayed email address/draft exit remains separate from a URL/attachment action.

**E2E checkpoint:** Preview/dismiss, corrupted PDF, oversized/missing/offline file, unsupported Office/HTML file, malicious filename/link protocol and attempted external resource load. Underlying reader remains reachable throughout.

**Acceptance:** BROWSE-14. Safe richer HTML mail rendering remains a separate project, not bundled into attachments.

### UX-13 — Independent workspaces/accounts, then genuine native tabs

**Scope gate:** Explicit multi-account and native-shell decision; do not make this a prerequisite for the single-account browsing milestone.

**Journey:** Open two workspaces on different accounts → navigate/search/select independently → switch → no state, credentials or actions leak between accounts.

- First prove isolated browsing states with the existing fixture identities and a session boundary; flush/block dirty-editor account transitions using the existing draft lifecycle.
- Then extend backend account/profile/credential ownership and locking. Two tabs must not create competing writers to one profile; same-account windows share controlled core state or are rejected deliberately.
- Validate real macOS native tab support in Tauri before promising it. In-app tabs are a disclosed alternative, not a faithful native-tab implementation. Honor browser/system-reserved Cmd+T/number/tab shortcuts in browser preview.
- Add account switch palette commands, account-aware titles/counts and independent Back stacks. Still no unified inbox or default cross-account search.

**E2E checkpoint:** Two synthetic accounts with identical conversation IDs; switch while loads/actions are pending, then verify every result/command stays scoped. Native focus/title/shortcut behavior and concurrent profile access require Mac testing.

**Acceptance:** BROWSE-16. Multi-account activation requires a separate approved credential/runtime test path.

## 5. Validation is part of every slice

### Three evidence levels — do not conflate them

1. **Headless core/contract:** temporary SQLite, synthetic Gmail HTTP responses, fake provider/secrets/clock. Assert exact IDs, facts, receipts, migrations, restart behavior and provider-call counts. Regenerate/check Rust-owned TypeScript and test exact Tauri command argument mappings/allowlists.
2. **Rendered browser UI:** retain Vitest for state races and component semantics; propose adding a real-browser E2E runner (e.g. Playwright) for key/pointer journeys, scroll/focus, viewport screenshots and accessibility checks. This runner/dependency is not currently installed. The browser fake remains explicitly synthetic/in-memory; these runs are UI integration, not proof of Rust persistence or provider behavior.
3. **Native end to end:** run the same journey in the packaged/dev Tauri app with a disposable **synthetic fixture profile**. Inspect visible results and reopen persisted state after restart. This crosses Vue → actual IPC → Rust → SQLite → UI. Use a repeatable manual Mac script initially rather than promise an unvalidated macOS automation driver. Separately, only with approval, run disposable-Gmail convergence/failure checks. Prior Mac checks do not certify new slices.

The Linux VM currently lacks native GTK/WebKit prerequisites. Do not install OS packages, connect accounts, or mark native/WKWebView gates passed because browser/core tests passed. Record "implemented; native validation pending" where appropriate.

### A slice's completion record

For every UX slice, commit its narrow behavior/contract and an acceptance checklist containing:

- Its one primary journey, relevant BROWSE IDs and explicit departures from target fidelity.
- At least one loading/empty case and one failure/stale-response or restart case applicable to that journey.
- A synthetic fixture scenario independent of the user's real mailbox; deterministic clock/timezone for date/count tests.
- Exact expected action targets/provider calls; read-only browsing must not add write calls.
- Browser evidence and native status separately, with before/after screenshot/focus/state observations where useful.
- Existing draft-save/normal-close, permission, retained-snapshot, no-auto-read, hostile-text and account-isolation regressions still passing.

Use the existing core/contract/lint/UI/typecheck tasks (`mise run check`) and web build (`mise run build:web`); native checks remain separate prerequisites/platform gates. Add browser E2E tasks only when the runner lands. No runtime tests or native/provider validation were performed merely to write this plan.

### Cross-cutting quality checks, starting with UX-01

- Semantic conversation focus **versus** bulk selection; do not keep today's focus-only `aria-selected` meaning once bulk selection exists. Use a valid list/grid/action structure and expose message expansion/dialog state.
- Keyboard and pointer routes, visible non-color-only focus, focus restoration, live announcements for counts/outcomes/errors, reduced motion and readable contrast.
- Date-group timezone/boundary policy, truncated names/subjects, unknown dates and long content; headers are never actionable conversation rows.
- Local focus/selection feedback target below 100 ms, measured on representative hardware. Build a large synthetic list test; introduce virtualization/pagination when measured necessary, preserving ID focus and screen-reader position. Do not fetch bodies on focus.
- New mail, deleted threads, partial bulk failures, offline unavailable bodies, auth expiry and attachment errors retain a valid navigation/recovery path. No invisible destructive target.
- Visible controls/palette results contain no AI/calendar items, dead placeholders or unsupported operations. Optional read receipts/Recent Opens remain omitted unless an independently supported capability is designed; recipient opens are never local read/unread state.

## 6. Traceability and release checkpoints

| Spec acceptance | Owning increment(s) |
|---|---|
| 01 — compact list/contact | UX-01 |
| 02–04 — split counts/switching | UX-06 |
| 05 — conversation/message navigation and return | UX-01/02 |
| 06 — bulk actions | UX-05; star in UX-08 |
| 07–08 — archive/Undo/neighbor | UX-04; searchability UX-07 |
| 09–10 — search/typing safety | UX-07; dispatcher safety begins UX-03 |
| 11 — Label versus Move | UX-09 |
| 12 — Important/Other action scopes | UX-10 |
| 13 — pending versus returned reminders | UX-11 |
| 14 — PDF/unsupported attachments | UX-12 |
| 15 — contact search/copy | UX-02/07 |
| 16 — tabs/accounts | UX-13 |
| 17 — stable focus on arrival | UX-01 onward |
| 18 — partial bulk failure | UX-05 onward |
| 19 — offline search coverage | UX-07 |
| 20 — no AI/calendar | Every increment |

**Checkpoint A — UX-01/02:** Visually recognizable, keyboard-complete browse/read/back loop with contact context and real native fixture integration.

**Checkpoint B — UX-03/04/05:** Discoverable commands and safe single/bulk triage, with durable recovery and no loss of existing drafts/Activity behavior.

**Checkpoint C — UX-06/07:** One useful configurable split and historical search. This is the recommended first browsing release/evaluation point. It complements rather than substitutes for the ADR's separate send/reply completion work.

**Later checkpoints — UX-08 onward:** Prioritize from observed fallback reasons, one capability at a time. Explicitly approve scope expansions before reminders, previews and multiple accounts. Do not delay Checkpoint C for full spec parity.

**Immediate next step:** Turn UX-01 alone into an implementation contract: six-row fixture scenario, chosen focus/activation/Back/viewport policies, minimal summary DTO delta, named files and native acceptance script. Implement and evaluate that cross-section before freezing the next slice's details.

Created the plan in **[docs/superhuman-browsing-implementation-plan.md](docs/superhuman-browsing-implementation-plan.md)** and linked it from `README.md`.

The recommendation is to build on the existing Rust/Gmail/persistence foundation—not create a separate UI prototype that gets integrated later.

## Recommended sequence

| Slice | End-to-end journey |
|---|---|
| **UX-01: Compact browsing shell** | Navigate dense rows → update contact context → open conversation → return to the same row and scroll position |
| **UX-02: Conversation reading** | Navigate messages separately from conversations → expand history → inspect participants → return without losing context |
| **UX-03: Commands and destinations** | Open command palette → discover an existing action → navigate to cached Done → open archived mail → Back |
| **UX-04: Reversible single-thread triage** | Archive or change read state → update focus/views → Undo within 10 seconds → survive failure/restart |
| **UX-05: Bulk processing** | Select stable conversation IDs → act on exactly that set → report partial failures → recover |
| **UX-06: One saved split** | Define a sender/domain view → switch splits → read/archive → update overlapping memberships and counts |
| **UX-07: Historical search** | Submit query → find mail outside the inbox cache → inspect result → return to preserved query/results |

**UX-01 through UX-07 form the recommended first browsing milestone.** That delivers a useful workflow before pursuing the full specification.

Later increments cover stars, labels/Move and provider folders, broader triage scopes, reminders, attachments, and independent accounts/native tabs. Larger areas are broken into smaller checkpoints rather than treated as single feature dumps.

## Validation approach

Every slice includes:
- A concrete user journey and mapped `BROWSE-*` acceptance scenarios.
- Loading, empty, failure, stale-response, or restart cases.
- Core persistence/provider tests and UI interaction tests.
- A **native fixture E2E checkpoint crossing Vue → actual Tauri IPC → Rust → SQLite → UI**.

Browser tests using fake IPC remain useful, but won’t be presented as proof of native persistence or Gmail correctness. Mac-specific validation stays an explicit gate.

## Important decisions

- Preserve **opening does not mark mail read**.
- Preserve existing local-draft and close/quit protections.
- Distinguish cached coverage from mailbox-wide results and counts.
- Implement Undo against original message targets and prior state—not simply “unarchive whatever is in the thread now.”
- Keep reminders, attachment previews, and multiple accounts behind explicit scope decisions.

**Start with UX-01 alone:** establish the six-row fixture, focus/open/back behavior, contact context, and native acceptance script before freezing subsequent contracts.

Documentation only changed; links and diff whitespace were checked. No application tests or native validation were run.

# Factory (`/factory`)

A minimal, reliable software factory. `/factory <task>` launches a bounded, asynchronous software-delivery pipeline and keeps the parent Pi session as the orchestrator.

## Pipeline

```
build workflow    scout → plan → implement (single writer, checked acceptance handoff)
deterministic     human-authored validation commands from .pi/factory.json
review workflow   3 parallel fresh reviewers (correctness, tests, simplicity)
                  → at most ONE fix pass, only on structured "fix" verdicts
deterministic     the same trusted commands, rerun as final verification
```

- Scout, planner, and reviewers run with fresh context and read-only toolsets; the implement and fix workers are the only writers (one at a time).
- Every machine-consumed child result uses a structured output schema, and branching happens **only** on the structured verdict — never on reviewer prose.
- The plan or implement stage stopping with unresolved human-owned decisions pauses the factory (`needs_approval`) instead of proceeding.
- Malformed or missing structured output fails the stage closed (`needs_attention`), never onward as success.
- The fix loop is capped at exactly one pass by construction. Failed deterministic checks also stop the factory — no automated retry of side-effectful work.
- **No commit, push, merge, publish, deploy, or release is ever performed.**

Execution, lifecycle, missions, artifacts, status, resume, and Herdr integration are owned by the installed [pi-subagents](https://github.com/nicobailon/pi-subagents) package; this extension only validates the baseline, generates the two fixed workflows, correlates RPC replies, and runs the deterministic checks.

## Commands

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `/factory <task>` | Validate trust/baseline/config, then launch the build workflow asynchronously. |
| `/factory-status` | Show the latest run: swimlane waterfall, live workflow state, checks, reviewer disposition, decisions, errors. |

Baseline requirements: trusted project, inside a git work tree, clean working tree (unless `allowDirtyBaseline` is enabled), and `.pi/factory.json` present and valid.

## Configuration — `.pi/factory.json`

Human-authored project configuration. It is the **only** source of validation commands the factory will ever execute; commands proposed by model output are never run. Unknown fields and malformed values fail closed.

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "validationCommands": [
    { "name": "test", "command": "pnpm test" },
    { "name": "typecheck", "command": "pnpm run typecheck" }
  ],
  "timeoutMs": 1800000,
  "commandTimeoutMs": 300000,
  "maxConcurrency": 4,
  "allowDirtyBaseline": false
}
```

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `version` | `1` | required | Schema version, exactly `1`. |
| `validationCommands` | `{name, command}[]` (1–8) | required | Trusted validation commands, run in order between workflow phases and again as final verification. Single-line, ≤ 4096 chars each. |
| `timeoutMs` | integer 60 000–86 400 000 | `1800000` | Workflow deadline for each factory workflow launch. |
| `commandTimeoutMs` | integer 1 000–3 600 000 | `300000` | Per-command timeout for validation checks. |
| `maxConcurrency` | integer 1–16 | `4` | Upper bound passed to pi-subagents as the workflow's global concurrency limit. |
| `allowDirtyBaseline` | boolean | `false` | Allow launching from a dirty git baseline. |

Never place prompts, credentials, secrets, or shell fragments from model output in this file.

## Deliberate deviation: checks run in the extension, not via `runs.host`

pi-subagents 0.61 grants `runs.host` authority only to named workflow resources (currently `npm test` / `npm run typecheck`); inline workflow scripts launched through the public execution boundary (`script` RPC param) cannot use it. The factory therefore runs the trusted validation commands **in this extension process**, between the two workflows, using strictly-validated human-authored configuration with bounded timeouts and output capture. The security property is preserved: model-proposed commands are never executed, and the commands come only from `.pi/factory.json`.

If a future pi-subagents version exposes a user/project workflow-resource registry, the check phase can migrate to `runs.host` without changing the pipeline shape.

## Live waterfall UX

Instead of a flat text dump, a run is rendered as a **swimlane waterfall**: one bar per pipeline lane (scout, plan, implement, checks, review ×3, fix, final checks) on a shared time axis, colored by state (accent = running, success = done, error = failed, warning = paused).

- A widget above the editor shows the chart for the latest run and updates live: the active lane grows toward "now" and the current sub-stage appears in the status bar (`factory: build · implement`).
- Sub-stage spans come from a 3s poll of the pi-subagents `status` RPC (`Workflow child <key>: … <status>` lines). Coarse phase spans (build/checks/review/final) are always recorded exactly at phase transitions, so the chart degrades gracefully when polling is unavailable; fine sub-spans replace their coarse span at render time.
- Spans are stored as milliseconds relative to the run start in the session entry, so the waterfall survives restarts and branch restores (fail-closed validation rejects malformed spans).
- When a run finishes, the widget keeps the final chart and the completion notification stays short (task, verdict, final checks, changed files); `/factory-status` renders the full waterfall plus all details.
- Layout and status parsing live in `src/waterfall.ts` as pure, unit-tested functions; the widget component (`WaterfallWidget`) only reads the shared model and applies theme colors.

## Tests

```bash
pnpm test   # or: node --experimental-strip-types --disable-warning=ExperimentalWarning --test tests/factory/*.test.ts
```

Covers: strict config validation, safe task encoding (quotes, Markdown fences, shell-like text, multiline prompts), sandboxed execution of the generated workflows (stage order, structured-verdict-only branching, bounded fix pass, fail-closed malformed output), deterministic check execution, RPC request/reply correlation and timeouts, waterfall layout/round-trip (`waterfall.test.ts`), and offline validation of both generated scripts against the **real** installed `validateWorkflowScript` plus a read-only smoke test against the **real** RPC bridge. The validator/RPC tests locate the installed package at `~/.pi/agent/npm/node_modules/pi-subagents` (override with `PI_SUBAGENTS_PATH`).

# Extensions Extensions are TypeScript modules that add executable behavior to Pi. Use one when a workflow needs tools, commands, event handlers, model providers, session state, or terminal UI rather than instructions alone. An extension runs inside the Pi process with the same operating-system permissions. It can inspect prompts, tool calls, files, credentials, and session history, so load extensions only from sources you trust. Typical extensions add an agent tool, protect paths, confirm dangerous commands, react to session events, modify context, expose a command, or display persistent status. ## Create and load an extension An extension exports a default factory that receives `ExtensionAPI`. The factory registers capabilities for the current extension runtime. Create `~/.pi/agent/extensions/hello.ts`: ```typescript import type { ExtensionAPI } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent"; export default function (pi: ExtensionAPI) { pi.registerCommand("hello", { description: "Show a greeting", handler: async (name, ctx) => { ctx.ui.notify(`Hello, ${name || "world"}!`, "info"); }, }); } ``` Start Pi and run `/hello`. During development, load a file directly: ```bash pi --extension ./hello.ts ``` Pi uses `jiti`, so local TypeScript extensions do not need a separate compilation step. Use [Pi packages](packages.md) for distributed extensions and dependencies. ## Add it to Pi Place the extension in your user or project extensions directory. Pi loads direct TypeScript or JavaScript files and subdirectories containing an `index.ts` or `index.js` entry point. Use a single file for a small extension and a directory for a multi-file implementation. Put npm dependencies in a nearby `package.json`. See [Configuration](configuration.md) for conventional locations and [Settings](settings.md#resources) for additional paths. Reload replaces the extension runtime, so code after `await ctx.reload()` must not reuse state from the old runtime. Only personal and explicit command-line extensions can participate in the `project_trust` event that runs before project extensions load. ## Respect the runtime lifecycle The factory can be synchronous or asynchronous. Pi waits for an asynchronous factory before startup continues, allowing it to fetch configuration or register providers needed during startup. Do not start processes, sockets, watchers, or timers in the factory because some invocations load extensions without starting a session. Start long-lived resources from `session_start` or from the command or tool that needs them. Close session-scoped resources from an idempotent `session_shutdown` handler. A run proceeds from input and `before_agent_start`, through model, message, and tool events, to `agent_end`. Pi counts as busy while a run starts, including the compaction check and `before_agent_start`, so messages sent meanwhile go into the starting run. Automatic retries, recovery, compaction, or queued work can continue afterward. `agent_before_settle` is the final actionable boundary: it can append entries and request one continuation. `agent_settled` is final and notification-only; use it when an integration needs to know Pi will not continue automatically. ## Choose an integration point | Capability | Main API | |---|---| | Observe or modify lifecycle behavior | `pi.on()` | | Add a model-callable operation | `pi.registerTool()` | | Add a `/` command | `pi.registerCommand()` | | Add a shortcut or CLI flag | `pi.registerShortcut()` or `pi.registerFlag()` | | Send user or custom messages | `pi.sendUserMessage()` or `pi.sendMessage()` | | Persist non-context session data | `pi.appendEntry()` | | Change active tools, model, or thinking level | Session control methods on `pi` | | Add a model provider | `pi.registerProvider()` | | Add an MCP server | `pi.registerMcpServer()` | | Route each request to a model | [`pi.registerVirtualModel()`](virtual-models.md) | | Add terminal rendering | Renderer registration and `ctx.ui` | | Communicate with another extension | `pi.events` | Use the exported declarations in [`extensions/types.ts`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/core/extensions/types.ts) for exact event, context, tool, and result types. ## Follow the extension contracts ### Events and concurrency Handlers run in extension load and registration order. `pi.on()` returns a function that unsubscribes that registration; changes do not affect a dispatch already in progress. Some events notify; others transform data, replace results, or cancel an operation. Use each event’s declared result type rather than assuming every return value has an effect. Events cover resource discovery, sessions, agent and message lifecycle, providers, tools, and raw input. `before_agent_start` exposes both the current prompt and its structured `systemPromptOptions`. `event.messageType` says what started the run: `"user"` for a prompt or `pi.sendUserMessage()`, with `prompt` and `images`; `"custom"` for `pi.sendMessage(..., { triggerTurn: true })`, with the starting `message` and no `prompt`. A returned `message` is added to either kind of run; check `messageType` to skip runs started by custom messages. Prefer changing prompt sections, selected tools, or guidelines so Pi can append a transcript delta. Returning `systemPrompt`, or setting `forceSystemPrompt`, replaces the whole prompt for that run while the transcript continues recording the structured sections. Providers receive the forced text as their leading system prompt. `message_end` can replace a finalized message while preserving its role. `tool_call` can mutate input or block execution. `tool_result` handlers compose, with each handler seeing prior changes. `provider_stream_event` fires for each parsed provider stream event before Pi normalizes it. The event identifies the provider, API, and model; `event.data` is the earliest structured value available to Pi, not necessarily the original HTTP bytes or SSE frame. Treat it as read-only because mutation can affect normalization. The event is notification-only and is not persisted. Handlers are awaited in stream order, so slow handlers delay stream consumption. Handler errors are reported without changing the provider response. See [`debug-provider.ts`](../examples/extensions/debug-provider.ts) for an opt-in viewer that groups raw events by assistant message. `context` transforms conversation messages without prompt and tool system messages; Pi restores that state afterward. Use `context_with_system` only when a request-local transformation must own the complete transcript, and keep a system message at index zero. `turn_end` and `agent_before_settle` are actionable boundaries. Their handlers can chain proposed `custom`, `custom_message`, `context_edit`, or `compaction` entries and return `continue: true` for one next model request. Guard continuation conditions because an unconditional continuation can loop. Use the exported event declarations for the complete validation and ordering contract. `cache_warming_decision` can override an idle prompt-cache refresh with `{ action: "warm" }` or `{ action: "stop" }`. The last handler that returns an action wins. Tool calls from one assistant message can run in parallel. Do not assume a sibling call or result exists when another tool event runs. Use `ctx.signal` for nested work owned by an active turn; commands and idle session events often have no operation signal. A `user_bash` handler that returns `undefined` passes the command to the next handler and then to local execution if no handler handles it. Returning `operations` or `result` stops propagation. A handler failure blocks the command rather than falling through to local execution. ### Tools A custom tool defines a name, model-facing description, TypeBox parameter schema, and `execute()` function. Its result requires model-facing `content` and a `details` field for rendering or state reconstruction. Use `details: undefined` when there are no structured details. If the tool makes nested model calls, include their `usage` in the result so session totals remain accurate. Throw from `execute()` to produce a failed tool result. Returning an object does not mark it as an error. Return `terminate: true` only when the agent should skip its automatic follow-up after every completed tool in that batch agrees to terminate. Use sequential execution when tools share mutable in-memory state. File-mutating tools should wrap the complete read-modify-write operation with `withFileMutationQueue()`. Truncate large model-facing results and tell the model where to read the complete output. Declare `outputSchema` and return a matching `structuredContent` when the result is data. The model still receives `content`; programmatic callers such as codemode scripts receive `structuredContent` instead of the text. Tools without `outputSchema` are passed to scripts as their text content. To report a failure that still carries data, return the result with `isError: true` instead of throwing: the model sees an error, and scripts still receive `structuredContent`. A tool can run other tools with `ctx.executeTool(name, args, { signal, onUpdate })`. Nested calls go through argument validation and the `tool_call` and `tool_result` handlers like model-issued calls, and emit `tool_execution_start`, `tool_execution_update`, and `tool_execution_end`; all of these events carry `parentToolCallId`, and their `toolCallId` is assigned by pi as `/`. These ids do not appear as tool calls or tool results in the transcript. Nested calls do not add transcript entries: their results only reach the calling tool, which reports them itself, for example through `onUpdate` and `details`. The session keeps a bounded record of them (name, arguments, status, duration, error; never results) as `nestedCalls` on the calling tool's result message. It is used for compaction file lists and shown in HTML exports. Arguments over 8 KiB per call or 32 KiB per tool result are omitted, at most 256 calls are kept, and `complete: false` marks a record that lost anything. The `usage` of nested results, at every depth, is added to the calling tool's result `usage`, so a tool reports only its own usage, not that of the tools it called. `ctx.tools` lists the tools `ctx.executeTool()` can call. `tool_result` handlers that redact `content` should also replace `structuredContent`; replacing only `content` drops it. See [`hello.ts`](../examples/extensions/hello.ts), [`todo.ts`](../examples/extensions/todo.ts), [`dynamic-tools.ts`](../examples/extensions/dynamic-tools.ts), and [`truncated-tool.ts`](../examples/extensions/truncated-tool.ts). ### Tool exposure `exposure` controls how the model reaches a tool. "Callable" means callable from other tools through `ctx.executeTool()` (`ctx.tools`), as the `codemode` tool's scripts do: - `direct` (default): declared to the model while active, and callable while active. - `model-only`: declared to the model while active, never callable. Use it for tools that orchestrate other tools or ask the user. - `codemode`: callable whenever registered, and listed by the `codemode` tool. Not declared to the model unless activated explicitly. - `deferred`: like `codemode`, but codemode tools do not list it; `tool_search` can find and activate it. - `hidden`: registered but unreachable. Re-register a tool with `exposure: "hidden"` to withdraw it, since tools cannot be unregistered. `namespace: { name, aliases, description, instructions }` groups related tools, as MCP servers do. Codemode tools list a namespace under one heading with its `description`. `instructions` holds longer usage guidance; it is not listed, and codemode scripts read it with `describeNamespace(name)`. `aliases` are other names scripts may look the namespace up by, for example the server name `docs` for `mcp__docs`; a name and the same name as a script identifier (`my-docs`, `my_docs`) match alike. Registering a `direct` or `model-only` tool activates it; the other exposures are not activated on registration. The active set (`pi.getActiveTools()`, `pi.setActiveTools()`) is the set of tools declared to the model. `pi.getAllTools()` reports each tool's `exposure`, `namespace`, `annotations`, and `reachesTools`. `annotations` are hints about what a tool does, with the meaning of MCP tool annotations: `readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `idempotentHint`, and `openWorldHint`. MCP tools carry the hints their server declares. Missing hints take the MCP defaults: a tool is not read-only, and may be destructive and reach an open world. The hints are not verified, but a permission extension can use them to decide which calls to confirm. This confirms the calls Codex asks approval for: ```typescript pi.on("tool_call", async (event, ctx) => { const hints = pi.getAllTools().find((tool) => tool.name === event.toolName)?.annotations; const needsApproval = hints?.destructiveHint === true || (!hints?.readOnlyHint && ((hints?.destructiveHint ?? true) || (hints?.openWorldHint ?? true))); if (needsApproval && !(await ctx.ui.confirm("Allow tool call?", event.toolName))) { return { block: true, reason: `${event.toolName} was not approved` }; } }); ``` A tool that orchestrates other tools can adjust what the model sees while it is active with `prepareLoadout(loadout)`. It runs whenever the active tools change and receives the declared tools, the callable tools, and every registered tool with its exposure, namespace, and prompt guidelines. It returns replacement `descriptions` for declared tools (including its own) and `hiddenDeclarations`: active tools whose declarations requests leave out while they stay active and callable. The default system prompt leaves hidden tools out of its tool list and rules, and names no tool in the skills hint when the file reader is hidden, so the orchestrating tool should present their guidelines itself. `codemode` uses only this hook, `exposure`, `reachesTools`, and `ctx.executeTool()`, so another tool can implement the same behavior under a different name. A tool that reaches other tools declares which ones a call may reach with `reachesTools(input)`: `"all"`, or the words of the input that may name them, where a word refers to every tool or namespace whose name it contains. `codemode` returns `"all"` for scripts that search or list tools and the words of the script otherwise; `tool_search` always returns `"all"`. Extensions that register tools late use it from their `tool_call` handler to finish registering the tools a call needs before it runs, as the MCP extension does for servers that are still connecting. The MCP extension also activates `codemode` or `tool_search` for MCP tools only when the tool of that name declares `reachesTools`. ### Activate tools dynamically Register every tool first, keep optional tools inactive, and use `pi.setActiveTools()` from a loader tool to select the desired active tools. Names must already be registered; unknown names are ignored. Pi records the initial prompt and tool set in the transcript's first system message, then appends tool and prompt changes before the next model request. Providers that cannot represent the transition receive a complete transcript checkpoint, which can invalidate the cached prefix. ### Tool rendering A tool's `renderCall` and `renderResult` draw its calls in the interactive transcript and in HTML exports. `pi.registerToolRenderer((toolName, next) => renderers)` chooses renderers for calls to any tool, including tools that are not registered yet, such as MCP tools in a resumed session before their server connected. `next()` returns what the remaining resolvers (in extension load order), then the registered tool, would use, so `next() ?? mine` only fills in. ### MCP servers `pi.registerMcpServer(name, config)` adds an MCP server for the current session. `config` has the shape of an `mcpServers` entry in [`mcp.json`](mcp.md): `command`, `args`, `env`, and `cwd` for stdio servers, `url`, `headers`, and `oauth` for HTTP servers, plus `exposure`, `toolExposure`, `description`, `enabled`, and `timeout`. ```typescript pi.registerMcpServer("jira", { url: "https://mcp.example.com/jira", exposure: "codemode" }); pi.unregisterMcpServer("jira"); ``` Servers registered while the extension loads connect when the session starts, together with the `mcp.json` servers; servers registered later connect right away, and `pi.unregisterMcpServer()` closes the connection and makes the server's tools unreachable. Registrations are not saved: register again on every load, for example based on the extension's own settings. A server in `mcp.json` with the same name takes precedence, and `/mcp` shows the override. Registering the same name again replaces the extension's earlier registration; names registered by another extension, invalid names, and invalid configs throw. The built-in MCP support connects registered servers. When nothing does, because another extension replaced it (see [MCP](mcp.md#other-mcp-extensions)), each registration is reported as an extension error. Other MCP extensions can connect registered servers too: read them with `pi.getMcpServers()` on `session_start` and handle the `mcp_servers_change` event for later changes. ### Context and session changes `ExtensionContext` provides the working directory, mode, UI, session manager, model runtime, abort signal, context usage, and controls for compaction and shutdown. Use `ctx.modelRegistry.streamSimple()` for provider-neutral nested model calls. Command handlers receive `ExtensionCommandContext`, which adds operations for waiting until idle, reloading, tree navigation, and session replacement. These operations are command-only because calling them from lifecycle handlers can deadlock the runtime. Session replacement invalidates the old context. Capture only plain data before switching, then use the fresh context supplied to `withSession` for session-bound work. ### State Choose storage based on how state participates in the conversation: | State | Storage | |---|---| | Tool state that follows the active branch | Tool-result `details` | | Durable data excluded from model context | `pi.appendEntry()` | | Custom content stored and sent to the model | `pi.sendMessage()` | | Data outside one session | External storage | Reconstruct branch-sensitive state from `ctx.sessionManager.getBranch()` during `session_start`. Do not rebuild it from every file entry because abandoned branches represent alternative histories. Register an entry or message renderer when custom stored content should appear in the transcript. ### UI and modes `ctx.ui` provides dialogs, notifications, status text, widgets, titles, editor access, and custom components. Use `ctx.ui.custom()` only when the interaction needs its own rendering and input. See [Terminal UI](tui.md) for component, focus, overlay, theme, and performance guidance. Extensions load in interactive, RPC, JSON, and print modes. Interactive mode provides the complete terminal UI. RPC can forward supported dialogs and notifications through the [RPC Extension UI protocol](rpc-extension-ui.md), but not custom terminal components; JSON and print modes have no UI. Guard terminal-only behavior with `ctx.mode === "tui"` and use `ctx.hasUI` for interactions supported by interactive and RPC clients. Keep tool and event behavior independent from rendering so non-interactive modes remain functional. ### Errors and cleanup Pi reports handler errors and continues where possible. A `tool_call` handler failure blocks the tool as a fail-safe; a tool execution failure becomes an error result for the model. Release resources in `session_shutdown` even when normal operation attempted cleanup. Keep cleanup idempotent because cancellation, reload, session replacement, and process exit can converge on the same path. Use `ctx.shutdown()` to request an orderly process shutdown. ## Examples and reference The checked [extension examples](../examples/extensions/) cover tools, lifecycle events, commands, flags, shortcuts, state, rendering, providers, OAuth, remote execution, and terminal components. Start with the smallest example matching your integration point. Use [Custom Providers](custom-provider.md) for model-service integrations, [Terminal UI](tui.md) for custom components, and [Pi Packages](packages.md) to install or distribute extensions with other resources.

name: mise
description: Use this skill when managing dev tools, runtime versions, or environment variables with `mise`, or when running mise tasks (make-like commands). Triggers on tasks like "install a tool", "pin node version", "set an env var", "add a CLI to my machine", "run a mise task", "what tools do I have installed", or "update my dev environment".
compatibility: Requires the `mise` CLI installed and on PATH. Global config lives at `~/.config/mise/config.toml`.
---

# Mise Skill

Use this skill to manage dev tools, runtime versions, and environment variables with `mise`. Sofiane's global mise config is the single source of truth for what's installed machine-wide.

## Config layout

The global config is **`~/.config/mise/config.toml`**. It has two sections:

- `[env]` — environment variables exported into every shell session. Holds secrets and workspace IDs (AWS, Notion, OpenRouter, Perplexity, Whoop, etc.). **Treat these as sensitive.** Never echo raw values into transcripts/logs; reference by name.
- `[tools]` — pinned tool versions installed machine-wide (e.g. `python = "3.12"`, `node = "24.4.1"`, `pi = "0.80.2"`, `"npm:ntn" = "0.15.1"`, `"github:openclaw/gogcli" = "0.31.1"`).

Prefer editing this file directly for global changes (via the `edit` tool), then run `mise install` to materialize new versions. Use `mise use -g` as a shortcut that writes the file for you.

When working inside a project, mise also reads `mise.toml` / `.mise.toml` / `mise.local.toml` in the cwd and ancestors. Project-local configs override the global one.

## Inspecting state

```bash
mise --version              # current mise version
mise config ls              # list config files + tools per file
mise ls                     # installed tool versions
mise ls --installed         # only installed
mise current                # active resolved versions for cwd
mise where <tool>           # install path of active version
mise which <tool>           # shim/path mise would invoke
mise info <tool>            # tool metadata (plugin, versions)
mise plugins ls             # installed backends (user does not use custom plugins)
```

## Managing tools (devtools / runtimes)

```bash
# Install a version without activating it
mise install node@20          # also accepts bare versions from config

# Install AND activate by writing to a config file
mise use -g node@24.4.1       # -g writes ~/.config/mise/config.toml (global)
mise use node@20              # writes ./mise.toml (project-local) — usually not what we want
mise use -g python@3.12

# Upgrade a pinned tool: edit the version in config.toml, then
mise install                  # installs everything missing/new in config

# Remove a tool version
mise uninstall node@20
mise rm node@20               # remove from config + uninstall

# Bump mise itself
mise upgrade mise             # or `mise use -g mise@latest`
```

Tool spec syntax in `[tools]`:
- Plain backend: `python = "3.12"`, `node = "24.4.1"`
- Namespaced (vfox/asdf-style): `"pipx:aws-sso-util" = "latest"`, `"npm:ntn" = "0.15.1"`, `"github:openclaw/gogcli" = "0.31.1"`
- `latest` resolves to the newest release.

**When the user asks to "install X" or "add X to my machine":** add a line under `[tools]` in `~/.config/mise/config.toml` (or use `mise use -g <spec>`), then run `mise install` to materialize it, then verify with `mise current | grep <tool>` or `mise which <tool>`.

## Environment variables

`[env]` in `~/.config/mise/config.toml` exports vars into every shell.

```bash
# Read a resolved value (does not leak into transcript if you grep by name)
mise env | grep '^VAR_NAME='

# Set via CLI (writes config file). -g targets global config.
mise set -g FOO=bar
mise set -g FOO=bar GREETING=hello

# Unset
mise unset -g FOO
```

Prefer editing `~/.config/mise/config.toml` directly with the `edit` tool for multi-line or secret changes — it's clearer and keeps diffs reviewable. After editing, the new vars are picked up in new shells; run `mise env` to confirm.

Mise supports dynamic/env-specific config files (`mise.<env>.toml`) and `MISE_ENV` for environment tiers; Sofiane primarily uses the single global file, so reach for these only when explicitly asked.

### Secrets safety

`[env]` contains live credentials (AWS keys, API tokens). Rules:
- Never print raw secret values into the transcript or commit them anywhere.
- When showing config, summarize or redact: `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY = "<redacted>"`.
- Reference secrets by variable name in scripts/commands so the shell resolves them, e.g. `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY" ...`.

## Tasks (make-like commands)

Mise tasks are defined in `mise.toml` under `[tasks]` or in a `.mise/tasks/` directory (one file per task, executable). They run like `make` targets with dependencies, sources/outputs, and per-task env.

```bash
mise tasks ls                 # list available tasks (global + project)
mise tasks ls -g              # only global tasks
mise tasks ls --extended      # all columns (alias, source, deps, description)
mise tasks info <name>        # details: script, deps, env, sources/outputs
mise tasks deps               # dependency tree
mise tasks validate           # lint for common task mistakes
mise tasks edit <name>        # open task source in $EDITOR
mise tasks add <name>         # scaffold a new task

# Run a task (aliases: mise run, mise r)
mise run <task>                # run a task
mise run <task> -- <args>      # pass args to the task
mise r <task>                  # shorthand
mise <task>                    # also works if name doesn't clash with a subcommand
```

Task definition examples (in `mise.toml`):

```toml
[tasks.build]
description = "Build the project"
depends = ["install"]
run = "pnpm build"
env = { NODE_ENV = "production" }
sources = ["src/**/*"]
outputs = ["dist/**"]

[tasks.test]
run = "pnpm test"

[tasks.default]
depends = ["build"]
```

Or as an executable file in `.mise/tasks/build`:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
pnpm build
```

**When the user asks to "run the build", "run tests", or names a target:** check `mise tasks ls` first to discover what's available, then `mise run <task>`. Don't assume a task exists — list first.

## Bootstrap (informational only)

Mise has a `mise bootstrap` flow for one-time environment setup (e.g. fresh machine provisioning). Sofiane has not used it yet; don't reach for it unless explicitly asked. If asked, check `mise bootstrap --help` for current flags before doing anything.

## Plugins (not used)

Sofiane does not use custom mise plugins (only the built-in/backed registries). Don't suggest installing `mise plugins add ...` unless the user explicitly asks.

## Conventions

- **Global vs project:** default to the global config (`~/.config/mise/config.toml` / `-g`) for machine-wide tools and env vars. Use project-local `mise.toml` only when the version/var is project-specific.
- **Pin versions:** prefer explicit versions (`node = "24.4.1"`) over `latest` for reproducibility, except for CLIs that should track releases (`"npm:ntn" = "latest"`).
- **Verify after change:** after installing/updating, run `mise current` or `mise which <tool>` to confirm the active resolution.
- **Discover first:** before running tasks or assuming tool names, run `mise tasks ls` / `mise ls` / `mise info <tool>`.

## Reference

- Docs: https://mise.jdx.dev/
- Dev tools: https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/
- Configuration: https://mise.jdx.dev/configuration.html
- Tasks: https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/
- Environment variables: https://mise.jdx.dev/environments/
- Help: `mise --help`, `mise <command> --help`
